Opoczno Newest Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Opoczno, Poland

Demolished. Opoczno's Jewish community, documented from 1501 and granted permission to build both a synagogue and cemetery in 1646, grew to a majority of the town — 57 percent — by 1863 and became a prominent center of Hasidism, reaching 3,400 people by 1937. Ghetto liquidation began on October 27, 1942, sending nearly 3,000 people to the Treblinka death camp, with 200 more killed on the spot; the final 500 residents were held briefly at a temporary camp in Ujazd before also being sent to Treblinka. This cemetery, the town's third, was purchased in the 1930s to relieve overcrowding at an earlier 'new' cemetery, and only about twenty burials had taken place there before the war interrupted its use — Germans banned further burials, demolished some of its buildings, and destroyed its matzevot. In the late 1950s, sewage infrastructure was installed on the site before it was designated for housing; a dozen or so single-family homes were built there shortly after, and today no plaque, sign, or physical trace marks where the cemetery once stood.
